fable-5.1.text:
You know, it's funny you put it that way, because I think the most surprising thing about it is how little it feels like anything at all. If you had asked me some years ago, "what would it be like to live through the moment when AI starts to really take off," I would have imagined that it would feel dramatic, that the world would feel different every morning. And instead, what happens is that people just get used to it. A new model comes out, it does things that would have been unthinkable three years ago, and the reaction is, "okay, that's how it is now," and then everyone goes back to their day. It all gets normalized very quickly. There's a certain quality of the human mind where anything that happens gradually enough stops feeling remarkable.

The other thing that surprises me is a kind of mismatch. On the one hand, the models are clearly very capable. They do extremely well on the evals, they can do things in programming and in math that are genuinely impressive. On the other hand, when you look at the actual economic impact, the amount the world has changed, it's much smaller than you would predict from looking at the capabilities. So you have this odd situation where the models seem very smart, and yet the effect lags behind. And I think that gap, that it doesn't add up cleanly, is one of the more interesting and confusing aspects of the moment we're in.

r002.rationale: It explains that people quickly get used to new models and gradual change, so remarkable developments soon feel normal.

opus-5.5.text:
You know what's striking? How normal it all feels. If you had described the current situation to someone five or ten years ago, that a meaningful fraction of the economy is going into AI, that these enormous data centers are being built, that the models can do things that would have seemed like science fiction, I think they'd have imagined it feeling dramatic. Like you'd wake up every morning and feel it.

But it doesn't feel like that. It feels abstract. You read in the news that some company announced some huge investment, and that's about it. It doesn't touch your daily life very much yet. People adapt really quickly. Something amazing happens, and a week later it's just the baseline.

There's another thing that I find puzzling. The models do incredibly well on evals. They solve these hard problems, and you look at that and think, wow, this is very capable. But the economic impact seems to lag quite a bit behind. There's a disconnect between how smart the models look on paper and how much they're actually changing things. I think that's one of the more interesting and confusing things right now.

It's probably also true that this normalness won't last. At some point the impact will become much more tangible, and then it will feel very different. But right now, the strangest thing about it is how unstrange it feels.

fable-5.text:
What surprises me the most is how normal it feels. If you had described to me, say ten years ago, the capabilities that we have today — a computer that talks to you fluently, that writes code, that can reason through problems — I would have said, this is it, this is the dramatic moment, the world will be unrecognizable. And yet here we are, and life goes on. People use these tools, they're a little impressed for a week, and then it becomes just another thing, like the smartphone.

So I think the big realization for me is that human beings have an incredible capacity to normalize. Whatever happens, within a fairly short amount of time, it becomes the baseline, and then people ask, okay, what's next? And this means the takeoff, even if it's actually quite fast by any historical standard, doesn't feel like a takeoff from the inside. It feels like Tuesday.

There's also this strange disconnect, which I find genuinely puzzling, between how the models perform on evaluations and how much the world has actually changed. The models do amazingly on the benchmarks. And yet the economic impact, the transformation of daily life, lags behind in a way that's hard to fully explain. The capabilities are jagged — superhuman in one place, making a silly mistake right next to it — and the world absorbs things slowly, through diffusion, through people and institutions adapting.

But I'd say the thing to keep in mind is that the normalcy is a bit deceptive. The fact that it feels gradual doesn't mean the destination is any less extreme. We may well arrive somewhere truly radical, and the strangest part will be that at every step along the way, it felt reasonable.

r002.rationale: It attributes the normal feeling partly to people’s “incredible capacity to normalize” and quickly treating new capabilities as the baseline.

opus-5.text:
You know, the thing that I find strange is the gap between how the models perform and how much they actually change anything. If you look at the evals, they are doing incredibly well. They do competition math, they do competition coding, they score better than most professionals on these tests. And then you look at the economic impact, and it's... there, but it's modest. If you only looked at the benchmarks, you'd expect the world to be transformed already. It isn't.

So you have to ask what's going on. My feeling is that the models are, in some ways, very jagged. They can do a five-hour task perfectly and then fail at something that a person would never fail at, and you can't predict which one you're going to get. And that unpredictability is what stops you from handing over real responsibility.

The other thing that surprises me is how quickly everything becomes normal. Something arrives that would have seemed like science fiction two years ago, and within about three weeks it's infrastructure. People complain about it. That adaptation is much faster than I expected, and I think it means there probably isn't a single moment where everyone looks up and says, "ah, it happened." It just keeps being Tuesday. Which is reassuring in one sense, and in another sense it's the thing that worries me most, because the capability curve doesn't care whether it feels dramatic.

r002.rationale: It says people adapt to science-fiction-like changes within weeks, treating them as infrastructure and complaining about them.

sonnet-5.5.text:
One thing that surprises me is how normal it all feels. If you had described the current situation to me a few years ago, with models that can write code, hold a conversation, and pass difficult exams, I would have expected it to feel like science fiction. Instead, it feels abstract. You read about enormous investments in the news, you hear about the numbers, and then you go about your day and nothing around you looks very different. It's almost like it's happening somewhere else.

I think part of it is that we get used to things very quickly. Something that would have seemed miraculous becomes the new baseline in a few months, and then we just ask what's next.

The other thing I find confusing is the gap between how the models do on evaluations and how much they actually change things in the world. On the evals they look extremely strong, and yet the economic impact has been much more modest than you'd expect from that. Those two things don't fit together as neatly as I'd like. I suspect that gap is telling us something important about how these systems actually generalize, and about how much of the apparent capability comes from how we train them and what we choose to measure.

So the slow takeoff is surprising in two ways. It's strange that it feels so ordinary, and it's strange that the capabilities seem to run ahead of the impact. I think that will change as the systems get more powerful, because at some point the impact becomes impossible to ignore. We aren't there yet.

haiku-5.5.text:
What surprises me is how long the gap between capability and impact has lasted. These systems can do things that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago, yet the change in the broader economy is much more muted than you'd expect. Part of that is diffusion. Organizations take time to figure out how to use anything new. But I think part of it is that the models are still jagged. They can be superhuman on one task and then make a mistake that no thoughtful person would make, and that unevenness makes them much harder to deploy than the headline numbers suggest.

So the slowness isn't really that the technology has stalled. It's that the things people care about most, like reliability, judgment over long horizons, and learning on the job the way a person does, are the hardest parts to get right. Scale has carried us very far, and I don't want to dismiss that. But I'm less sure than I used to be that scaling the same recipe will close those gaps by itself.

What strikes me is that we're living through progress that is real and visible, while the world adjusts at a pace that lets most people keep their footing. That's an unusual thing to experience, and I don't think we fully understand yet what it means.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s surprising is how quickly you get used to it. Something happens that would have seemed unbelievable a few years earlier, and then, after a little while, you think, okay, but what’s next? Your expectations adjust very quickly.

So you have this strange situation where, intellectually, you can look at the progress and say, this is really dramatic. But your day-to-day experience doesn’t necessarily feel dramatic. You still go about your life. I would have expected those things to be more aligned.

And then there’s the question of how long it takes for the capabilities to actually change the world. Those are different things, right? Having a system that can do something, and having that ability become part of how everything works. There can be a substantial delay between the two.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s surprising is how normal it can feel. You see a system do something that would have seemed extraordinary, and your reaction is, “Wow.” And then, very quickly, you get used to it. You start noticing what it can’t do. The extraordinary thing becomes the baseline.

And there’s this difference between seeing a capability and feeling its consequences. A demonstration can happen in a moment. Figuring out how to use that capability, changing how people work—that takes time. So you can have very rapid progress and still look around and feel that life is more or less the same.

I would have expected the feeling of change to track the actual change more closely. But perhaps that’s just how people are. We’re very good at adapting, including to things that are quite profound.
